learn.hook: To dig a well from Delhi to the centre of the Earth, you would have to dig more than 6,000 km. Nobody has dug even 13 km! So how do we know what is inside?
points: The Earth has three main layers: the crust (outermost), the mantle (middle) and the core (centre).
The crust is the thin, rocky skin we live on. It is thinnest under the oceans (about 5 km) and much thicker under the continents, thickest below big mountains like the Himalayas.
Continental crust is mostly silica and alumina (called sial). Oceanic crust is mostly silica and magnesium (called sima). The core is mostly nickel and iron (called nife).

The mantle goes down to about 2,900 km. It is the largest layer by volume. The upper part of the mantle that is weak and slowly flowing is called the asthenosphere; the crust and the rigid top of the mantle together form the lithosphere.
The core has a liquid outer core and a solid inner core. Scientists learnt this from earthquake (seismic) waves: S waves cannot travel through liquids, and they do not pass through the outer core.

example.q: Think it through: The deepest hole ever drilled is only about 12 km deep. How can scientists still say the outer core is liquid?
steps: Earthquakes send seismic waves through the whole Earth, and seismographs around the world record them.
P waves can move through solids and liquids, but S waves can move only through solids.
S waves are not recorded on the far side of the Earth from an earthquake, because they are stopped at the outer core.
So the outer core must be liquid. These indirect clues, along with meteorites, volcanoes and gravity readings, tell us about the inside.
example.answer: By studying how seismic waves travel; S waves cannot pass through the outer core, so it must be liquid.

learn.reallife: Think of a mango: the thin skin is like the crust, the thick juicy pulp is like the mantle and the hard seed is like the core.

quiz.q: Which is the outermost layer of the Earth?
quiz.explain: The crust is the thin rocky outer layer on which we live, and it lies above the mantle.

The crust is the outermost, thin rocky layer on which we live.
Answer: Crust
quiz.mistake: Mixes up the order of the layers

quiz.q: Where is the Earth's crust thinnest?
quiz.explain: Oceanic crust is only about 5 km thick, while continental crust is much thicker, especially under high mountains.
steps: Oceanic crust is only about 5 km thick.
Continental crust is much thicker, so the crust is thinnest under the oceans.
Answer: Under the oceans
quiz.mistake: Thinks the crust has the same thickness everywhere

quiz.q: The Earth's core is made mainly of which two metals?
quiz.explain: The core is called nife because it is made mainly of nickel (Ni) and iron (Fe).
steps: The core is called nife.
Ni stands for nickel and Fe for iron.
Answer: Nickel and iron
quiz.mistake: Confuses the materials of the core with those of the crust (sial and sima)

quiz.q: Which part of the Earth is liquid?
quiz.explain: The outer core is liquid. The inner core is solid because the huge pressure there keeps it solid even though it is very hot.
steps: The core has a liquid outer part and a solid inner part.
So the liquid part is the outer core.
Answer: The outer core
quiz.mistake: Assumes that the hottest, deepest part must be the liquid one

quiz.q: Which layer of the Earth is the largest by volume?
quiz.explain: The mantle stretches from below the crust to about 2,900 km deep, so it holds the largest share of the Earth's volume.
steps: The mantle reaches down to about 2,900 km.
That makes it the largest layer by volume.
Answer: Mantle
quiz.mistake: Thinks the core is the biggest because it sits at the centre

quiz.q: What is the lithosphere?
options: The crust together with the rigid uppermost part of the mantle
The layer of air around the Earth
quiz.explain: The lithosphere is the solid, rigid outer shell: the crust plus the top part of the mantle. It is broken into plates.
steps: The crust and the rigid top of the mantle form one solid shell.
This shell is the lithosphere, broken into plates.
Answer: The crust together with the rigid uppermost part of the mantle
quiz.mistake: Thinks the lithosphere means only the crust or confuses it with the atmosphere

quiz.q: Why do scientists say S waves prove that the outer core is liquid?
options: S waves travel fastest through liquids
S waves are produced only inside the core
S waves can be seen on the surface of the core
S waves cannot travel through liquids, and they do not pass through the outer core
quiz.explain: S waves move only through solids. Because they are stopped at the outer core, that layer must be liquid.
steps: S waves can travel only through solids.
They do not pass through the outer core, so the outer core must be liquid.
Answer: S waves cannot travel through liquids, and they do not pass through the outer core
quiz.mistake: Mixes up the properties of P waves and S waves

quiz.q: The mantle extends to a depth of about how many kilometres?
quiz.explain: The mantle begins below the crust and continues to about 2,900 km, where the outer core starts.
steps: The mantle begins below the crust.
It goes down to about 2,900 km, where the outer core starts.
Answer: 2,900 km
quiz.mistake: Confuses the depth of the mantle with the thickness of the crust or the radius of the Earth

teach.ask: Gappu taps the ground with his beak: "Is the Earth solid rock all the way down? What is inside it?"
teach.praise: Wow! A thin crust, a thick mantle and a nickel-iron core with a liquid outer part. The Earth is like a giant mango!
teach.nudge: You told me the layers, but which part is liquid, and what is the core made of?

revise.summary: The Earth has three layers: the thin crust, the thick mantle and the core. The crust is thinnest under oceans. The core has a liquid outer part and a solid inner part, which scientists learnt from seismic waves.

learn.hook: Look at a world map: the bulge of Brazil seems to fit into the curve of West Africa like jigsaw pieces. Is that just luck?
points: In 1912, Alfred Wegener proposed the continental drift theory: all continents were once joined in one supercontinent called Pangaea, surrounded by a huge ocean called Panthalassa.
Pangaea split into Laurasia in the north and Gondwanaland in the south, which later broke into today's continents. India was part of Gondwanaland.

Evidence: the coastlines of South America and Africa fit; rocks of the same age match across the Atlantic; fossils of the same reptile, Mesosaurus, are found in both South Africa and Brazil; old glacial deposits (tillite) are found in India and other southern lands.

Plate tectonics explains the movement: the lithosphere is broken into large plates that move slowly, a few centimetres a year, over the asthenosphere. There are seven major plates and many minor ones.

Plates meet at three kinds of boundaries: divergent (move apart, e.g. Mid-Atlantic Ridge), convergent (move towards each other, e.g. Himalayas) and transform (slide past each other, e.g. San Andreas Fault).

example.q: Think it through: Why are the Himalayas called young fold mountains that are still rising?
steps: The Indian plate broke away from Gondwanaland and moved north towards Asia.
When the Indian plate pushed into the Eurasian plate, the layers of rock and sea-floor sediment between them were squeezed and folded upwards.
This happened only tens of millions of years ago, which is recent in the Earth's history, so the Himalayas are young.
The Indian plate is still pushing north, so the Himalayas are still rising and the region still has earthquakes.
example.answer: Because they formed recently from the collision of the Indian and Eurasian plates, which is still going on.

learn.reallife: The Himalayas, the earthquakes in north and north-east India, and even fossils of sea shells found high up in the Himalayas are all results of moving plates.

games.title: Drifting continents: true or false?
items: Alfred Wegener proposed the continental drift theory in 1912.
Wegener, a German scientist, put forward the idea in 1912.
Pangaea was the name of the huge ocean around the supercontinent.
Pangaea was the supercontinent; the ocean around it was Panthalassa.
India was once part of Gondwanaland.
India, Africa, South America, Australia and Antarctica were parts of Gondwanaland.
Tectonic plates move many kilometres every year.
Plates move only a few centimetres a year, about as fast as your fingernails grow.
Fossils of Mesosaurus are found in both South Africa and Brazil.
This reptile could not have crossed an ocean, so the two lands must once have been joined.
Forces from inside the Earth that build mountains are called endogenic forces.
Endogenic forces come from within the Earth; exogenic forces like rivers and wind act on the surface and wear land down.

quiz.q: What name did Wegener give to the single supercontinent that once existed?
quiz.explain: Pangaea means 'all earth'. Panthalassa, meaning 'all water', was the ocean around it.
steps: Wegener said all continents were once joined.
He called the supercontinent Pangaea; Panthalassa was the ocean around it.
Answer: Pangaea
quiz.mistake: Confuses the supercontinent with the ocean that surrounded it

quiz.q: India was once part of which southern landmass?
quiz.explain: Gondwanaland was the southern part of Pangaea and included India, Africa, South America, Australia and Antarctica.
steps: Pangaea split into Laurasia (north) and Gondwanaland (south).
India was part of Gondwanaland.
Answer: Gondwanaland
quiz.mistake: Mixes up the northern landmass Laurasia with the southern one

quiz.q: Which of these is evidence for continental drift?
options: Rivers flowing from mountains to the sea
Fossils of the same reptile, Mesosaurus, in South Africa and Brazil
Snow on the peaks of the Himalayas
Day and night on the Earth
quiz.explain: A small freshwater reptile could not cross an ocean, so finding its fossils on both sides shows the continents were once joined.
steps: Mesosaurus was a small reptile that could not cross an ocean.
Its fossils in both South Africa and Brazil show the continents were once joined.
Answer: Fossils of the same reptile, Mesosaurus, in South Africa and Brazil
quiz.mistake: Picks a common natural event that has nothing to do with moving continents

quiz.q: At a divergent boundary, the plates:
quiz.explain: At divergent boundaries plates pull apart and new crust forms from rising magma, as at the Mid-Atlantic Ridge.
steps: Divergent means going apart.
At divergent boundaries plates move away from each other, as at the Mid-Atlantic Ridge.
Answer: move away from each other
quiz.mistake: Confuses divergent with convergent boundaries

quiz.q: The Himalayas were formed mainly by:
options: a volcano erupting for millions of years
the collision of the Indian plate with the Eurasian plate
two plates sliding past each other
rivers depositing sand in the plains
quiz.explain: The Indian plate moved north and pushed into the Eurasian plate. The rock layers between them folded up to form the Himalayas.
steps: The Indian plate moved north into the Eurasian plate.
The rock layers between them folded up into the Himalayas.
Answer: the collision of the Indian plate with the Eurasian plate
quiz.mistake: Thinks all tall mountains are volcanoes

quiz.q: The San Andreas Fault in California is an example of which kind of plate boundary?
quiz.explain: Along the San Andreas Fault the Pacific and North American plates slide past each other sideways, which is a transform boundary.
steps: Along the San Andreas Fault two plates slide past each other sideways.
That is a transform boundary.
Answer: Transform boundary
quiz.mistake: Does not know that plates can also slide sideways past each other

quiz.q: About how fast do tectonic plates usually move?
options: They do not move at all
quiz.explain: Plates move very slowly, usually a few centimetres a year, but over millions of years this adds up to thousands of kilometres.
steps: Plates move very slowly over the asthenosphere.
Their speed is a few centimetres a year.
Answer: A few centimetres a year
quiz.mistake: Imagines plate movement is fast enough to see or that plates are fixed

quiz.q: How many major tectonic plates is the lithosphere usually divided into?
quiz.explain: The lithosphere has seven major plates, such as the Pacific, Eurasian and Indo-Australian plates, plus several minor plates.
steps: The lithosphere is broken into large plates.
There are seven major plates and many minor ones.
Answer: 7
quiz.mistake: Guesses a number without recalling the seven major plates, or adds the minor plates as well

teach.ask: Gappu is puzzled: "My atlas shows the continents far apart. How can people say they were once stuck together and are still moving?"
teach.praise: Chirp! The continents were once one Pangaea, and the plates still drift a few centimetres a year. The fossils and the jigsaw fit prove it!
teach.nudge: Good start! But what proof do we have that the continents were joined, and what is it that actually moves?

revise.summary: Wegener's continental drift theory (1912) said all continents were once one supercontinent, Pangaea. Plate tectonics explains that the lithosphere is broken into plates that move slowly and meet at divergent, convergent and transform boundaries.
focus: Continental drift — Pangaea, Laurasia and Gondwanaland
Plate tectonics and the three kinds of plate boundaries
remember: Wegener, 1912: Pangaea surrounded by Panthalassa; India was part of Gondwanaland
Evidence: matching coastlines, rocks, Mesosaurus fossils, tillite
Seven major plates moving a few centimetres a year
Divergent: Mid-Atlantic Ridge; convergent: Himalayas; transform: San Andreas Fault
traps: Pangaea was the land; Panthalassa was the ocean.
Transform plates slide past each other; convergent plates move towards each other.

learn.hook: The Earth shakes many times every day, but most quakes are so tiny that only machines notice them. What makes the ground shake?
points: An earthquake is a sudden shaking of the ground. It happens when rocks along a fault, usually near plate boundaries, suddenly slip and release stored energy.
The point inside the Earth where the slip starts is the focus (hypocentre). The point on the surface directly above it is the epicentre, where shaking is usually strongest.
Energy travels as seismic waves: P waves arrive first, then S waves, and surface waves arrive last and do the most damage.
A seismograph records the waves. Magnitude (energy released) is measured on the Richter scale; intensity (damage and shaking felt) on the Mercalli scale, which runs from 1 to 12.
The Himalayan region, the north-east and the Kachchh region of Gujarat are among the most earthquake-prone parts of India. A strong earthquake struck Bhuj in Gujarat on 26 January 2001.

example.q: Think it through: Your school is in an earthquake-prone town. When the shaking starts, what should you do and why?
steps: Do not run out while the ground is shaking, because falling objects and glass are the biggest danger.
DROP to your knees, take COVER under a strong desk and HOLD ON to it until the shaking stops.
Keep away from windows, shelves and anything that can fall. Do not use the lift.
When the shaking stops, walk out calmly with your teacher to an open ground away from buildings, trees and electric wires.
example.answer: Drop, cover and hold on until the shaking stops, then move calmly to an open area.

learn.reallife: Schools in India hold earthquake drills, and engineers design earthquake-resistant buildings with strong frames for hilly and quake-prone areas.

items: Stress builds up in rocks along a fault
Rocks suddenly slip at the focus

quiz.q: The place inside the Earth where an earthquake starts is called the:
quiz.explain: The focus, or hypocentre, is the point underground where rocks first slip. The epicentre is on the surface above it.
steps: Rocks first slip at a point underground.
That point is the focus (hypocentre); the epicentre is on the surface above it.
Answer: Focus
quiz.mistake: Confuses the focus with the epicentre

quiz.q: Where is the shaking of an earthquake usually strongest?
options: Exactly opposite on the other side of the Earth
Only at the focus deep underground
quiz.explain: The epicentre is the surface point closest to the focus, so the waves reach it with the most energy.
steps: The epicentre is the surface point directly above the focus.
Waves reach it with the most energy, so shaking is strongest there.
Answer: Near the epicentre
quiz.mistake: Thinks shaking increases with distance from the source

quiz.q: Which seismic waves cause the most damage on the surface?
quiz.explain: Surface waves travel along the ground, arrive last and shake buildings the most.
steps: P waves arrive first, then S waves, and surface waves last.
Surface waves travel along the ground and do the most damage.
Answer: Surface waves
quiz.mistake: Thinks the fastest wave must be the most damaging

quiz.q: Which instrument records earthquake waves?
quiz.explain: A seismograph records the waves produced by an earthquake. A barometer measures air pressure.
steps: Earthquake waves need a special recording instrument.
A seismograph records them; a barometer measures air pressure.
Answer: Seismograph
quiz.mistake: Mixes up instruments used for weather with those used for earthquakes

quiz.q: On the Richter scale, each step up of 1 means the ground motion recorded is how many times larger?
quiz.explain: The Richter scale goes up in steps of ten: a magnitude 6 earthquake makes waves 10 times larger than a magnitude 5 one.
steps: The Richter scale goes up in steps of ten.
So each step of 1 means ground motion 10 times larger.
Answer: 10
quiz.mistake: Thinks the scale goes up in equal small steps like a ruler

quiz.q: Most earthquakes happen:
options: only in places with very hot weather
quiz.explain: Plates push, pull or slide along their edges, so stress builds up and is released there as earthquakes.
steps: Stress builds up where plates push, pull or slide.
So most earthquakes happen along plate boundaries.
Answer: along plate boundaries
quiz.mistake: Thinks earthquakes are linked to weather or happen randomly anywhere

quiz.q: During an earthquake you are inside a classroom. What is the safest thing to do?
options: Run down the stairs at once
Get under a strong desk and hold on
Stand near the window to watch
Take the lift to the ground floor
quiz.explain: Drop, cover and hold on protects you from falling objects. Running, windows and lifts are all dangerous during shaking.
steps: During shaking, falling objects are the main danger.
So drop, get under a strong desk and hold on.
Answer: Get under a strong desk and hold on
quiz.mistake: Believes running outside during the shaking is safest

quiz.q: Which part of India is among the most earthquake-prone?
quiz.explain: The Himalayas lie where the Indian plate pushes into the Eurasian plate, so the region has frequent earthquakes.
steps: The Himalayas lie where the Indian plate pushes into the Eurasian plate.
So the Himalayan region is among India's most earthquake-prone areas.
Answer: The Himalayan region
quiz.mistake: Does not connect earthquakes with plate boundaries

teach.ask: Gappu's nest wobbled last night: "Was that an earthquake? Why does the ground shake, and what should I do next time?"
teach.praise: Tweet! Rocks slip at the focus, waves spread out and shake the epicentre most. And next time I will drop, cover and hold on!
teach.nudge: Hmm, what is happening deep underground to start the shaking, and how do I stay safe?

revise.summary: An earthquake is sudden shaking when rocks along a fault slip and release energy. It starts at the focus and is strongest near the epicentre. Seismographs record the waves; the Himalayas, the north-east and Kachchh are earthquake-prone parts of India.
focus: Measuring earthquakes — Richter and Mercalli scales
remember: Focus (hypocentre) is underground; epicentre is the surface point above it
P waves first, S waves next, surface waves last and most damaging
Richter scale = magnitude; Mercalli scale (1 to 12) = intensity
traps: The epicentre is on the surface, not deep inside the Earth.
Richter measures energy released; Mercalli measures damage and shaking felt.

learn.hook: India has an active volcano! It sits on an island in the Andaman Sea and has puffed out ash even in this century.
points: A volcano is an opening (vent) in the crust through which molten rock, gases, ash and rock pieces come out. Molten rock is called magma below the surface and lava once it comes out.
Volcanoes can be active (erupting now or recently), dormant (quiet for a long time but may erupt again) or extinct (not expected to erupt again).
Most volcanoes are near plate boundaries. The 'Ring of Fire' around the Pacific Ocean has many active volcanoes and earthquakes.
Barren Island in the Andaman and Nicobar Islands is India's only active volcano.
Lava builds new land. The Deccan Traps of Maharashtra were formed by huge lava flows from cracks; the basalt rock broke down into fertile black soil, which is good for cotton.

example.q: Think it through: Volcanoes can be dangerous, yet many farmers live on their slopes. Why?
steps: Volcanic ash and lava contain many minerals.
Over time they break down into very fertile soil that grows good crops.
Volcanic areas can also give hot springs and geothermal energy, and valuable minerals.
So people accept the risk, and scientists watch active volcanoes to warn them before an eruption.
example.answer: Volcanic material forms very fertile soil, and volcanoes also provide minerals and geothermal energy.

learn.reallife: The black soil of Maharashtra and Gujarat that grows cotton comes from ancient lava of the Deccan Traps.

quiz.q: What is lava?
options: Molten rock that stays deep inside the Earth
Molten rock that has come out on the Earth's surface
quiz.explain: Molten rock is called magma while it is underground and lava once it pours out on the surface.
steps: Molten rock is called magma underground.
Once it comes out on the surface it is called lava.
Answer: Molten rock that has come out on the Earth's surface
quiz.mistake: Uses magma and lava as if they meant the same thing

quiz.q: Where is India's only active volcano?
options: Barren Island, Andaman and Nicobar Islands
quiz.explain: Barren Island in the Andaman Sea is India's only active volcano. The others listed are mountains, not active volcanoes.
steps: India has only one active volcano.
It is Barren Island in the Andaman and Nicobar Islands.
Answer: Barren Island, Andaman and Nicobar Islands
quiz.mistake: Assumes any famous mountain could be a volcano

quiz.q: A volcano that has not erupted for a very long time but may erupt again is called:
quiz.explain: Dormant means 'sleeping'. An extinct volcano is not expected to erupt again at all.
steps: Active volcanoes erupt now; extinct ones are not expected to erupt again.
A volcano quiet for long but able to erupt again is dormant.
Answer: Dormant
quiz.mistake: Confuses dormant with extinct

quiz.q: The 'Ring of Fire' is found around which ocean?
quiz.explain: Many plate boundaries surround the Pacific Ocean, so it is ringed by volcanoes and earthquake zones.
steps: The Ring of Fire has many active volcanoes and earthquakes.
It lies around the Pacific Ocean.
Answer: Pacific Ocean
quiz.mistake: Picks the ocean nearest to India instead of recalling the Pacific

quiz.q: The Deccan Traps were formed by:
options: huge flows of lava that spread over the land
quiz.explain: Long ago, lava poured out of cracks again and again and hardened into thick layers of basalt called the Deccan Traps.
steps: Lava poured out of cracks again and again in Maharashtra.
It hardened into thick basalt layers called the Deccan Traps.
Answer: huge flows of lava that spread over the land
quiz.mistake: Does not know that plateaus can be built by lava

quiz.q: Black soil, good for growing cotton, formed mainly from which rock?
quiz.explain: Black soil (regur) formed from the weathering of basalt of the Deccan Traps.
steps: The basalt of the Deccan Traps broke down over time.
It formed fertile black soil, good for cotton.
Answer: Basalt
quiz.mistake: Does not link black soil with its volcanic parent rock

quiz.q: Why are most volcanoes found near plate boundaries?
options: The Sun is hottest over plate boundaries
Plate boundaries always lie in deserts
Rain falls most heavily over plate boundaries
Magma rises more easily where plates pull apart or one plate sinks under another
quiz.explain: At plate boundaries the crust is cracked or melting, which gives magma a path to the surface.
steps: At plate boundaries the crust is cracked or melting.
So magma rises more easily where plates pull apart or one sinks under another.
Answer: Magma rises more easily where plates pull apart or one plate sinks under another
quiz.mistake: Links volcanoes to surface heat or weather instead of the Earth's interior

quiz.q: Which of these is a benefit of volcanoes?
quiz.explain: Volcanic ash forms rich soil, and the heat below volcanic areas can be used as geothermal energy.
steps: Volcanic material forms rich soil.
Heat below volcanic areas also gives geothermal energy.
Answer: Fertile soil and geothermal energy
quiz.mistake: Thinks volcanoes have only harmful effects

teach.ask: Gappu peeks at a picture of a volcano: "Is that a mountain on fire? Where does all that red stuff come from?"
teach.praise: Squawk! Magma from deep inside pushes up through a vent and comes out as lava, usually near plate boundaries. Not fire at all!
teach.nudge: But where does the red stuff come from, and what do we call it before and after it comes out?

revise.summary: A volcano is a vent through which magma, gases and ash come out. Volcanoes may be active, dormant or extinct, and most lie near plate boundaries like the Ring of Fire. Barren Island is India's only active volcano, and lava built the Deccan Traps.
focus: Where volcanoes occur — plate boundaries and the Ring of Fire
Volcanoes in India and their benefits
remember: Magma below the surface, lava above it
Barren Island (Andaman and Nicobar) — India's only active volcano
Ring of Fire surrounds the Pacific Ocean
Deccan Traps basalt → black soil, good for cotton
traps: Dormant means sleeping but able to erupt; extinct means not expected to erupt again.
